design_detail: Systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis with meta-regression (registered on the Open Science Framework, 10.17605/OSF.IO/EJX5Q) of controlled experimental studies in healthy adults aged 18 to 70 that gave a measured dose of alcohol before a night of sleep measured by polysomnography. 27 studies included, all crossover designs except two; pooled mean differences against control for sleep onset latency, total sleep time, REM sleep onset latency, latency to deep (N3) sleep, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and sleep stages, with 95% prediction intervals; meta-regression on alcohol dose (g per kg), timing and the proportion of women; subjective sleep summarized narratively. Same team and methods as the caffeine meta-analysis (Gardiner et al., 2023).
can_establish: The average change in that night's objectively measured sleep after drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people without alcohol, in healthy adults in laboratory studies, and how the REM and sleep-onset effects change with the amount of alcohol.
cannot_establish: Effects of drinking earlier in the day (almost all studies gave alcohol within three hours of bedtime), of real-world nights out (later bedtimes, more alcohol, other drugs), in people with alcohol use disorder, insomnia, adolescents or adults over 70; whether men and women differ (only one study analysed sex); or whether alcohol changes total sleep time, sleep efficiency or night-time waking, for which the intervals and prediction intervals are wide.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies: laboratory volunteers, from 1 to 95 per study, published from 1966 to 2022 (Table 2, PDF pages 43-47, which carry no printed page numbers).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults 18 to 70; controlled experimental design; measured alcohol dose; night-time sleep measured after drinking; excluded naps under 90 minutes, alcohol more than 18 hours before or after the start of sleep, no sleep measures (pre-proof p. 6, lines 141-149). English-language peer-reviewed human studies only (lines 130-132).
sample.demographics: 12 studies men only, 4 women only, 11 mixed (45.3% men in the mixed studies) (pre-proof p. 16, lines 399-401); mostly young adults.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; several studies' data were excluded from pooling (missing variances, combined stages, implausibly small variances, part-night data) (pre-proof pp. 8-9, lines 194-205).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy laboratory volunteers drinking measured amounts shortly before a fixed bedtime, mostly vodka or other spirits with juice or tonic: real nights of drinking (later bedtimes, larger and uneven amounts, food, other drugs) are not represented.

exposure.measurement: Alcohol given as a measured dose in each study; doses in g per kg calculated by the authors for six studies (pre-proof p. 9, lines 205-208).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 37 alcohol conditions from 0.16 to 1.20 g per kg, classified as low (0.50 g per kg or less; 12 conditions), moderate (over 0.50 to under 0.75; 8) and high (0.75 or more; 17); the authors equate these to about three or fewer, three to five and five or more standard drinks of 10 g for a 62-kg adult (pre-proof pp. 10-11, lines 249-256). Mostly drunk within three hours of bedtime; four studies gave alcohol on two, three or nine nights (lines 256-258). Thresholds reported by the authors' dose models (results, not advice): REM onset delayed from about 0.35 g per kg, REM duration reduced from about 0.50, sleep onset shortened from about 0.85, latency to N3 shortened from about 0.95 (pre-proof pp. 12-14).
exposure.polysubstance: Beverage types varied (vodka, scotch, bourbon, beer, sake, shochu); the authors name this as a possible confounder (pre-proof p. 31, lines 757-758).

comparison.controls: The same participants without alcohol (placebo or no alcohol) in crossover studies; separate control groups in two studies.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison in most studies; time in bed standardized in only a few studies (pre-proof p. 19, lines 465-466; p. 26, lines 639-641).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception, drinking history and ADH genotype not accounted for in most studies (pre-proof pp. 28-31).

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography for objective sleep; questionnaires, diaries and visual analogue scales for subjective sleep (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard sleep scoring; slow-wave sleep and stages 3 and 4 combined as N3 following current guidelines (pre-proof p. 8, lines 186-189).
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disruption as changes in latency, total sleep, waking and stage durations or proportions.

analysis.effect_sizes: Multilevel mixed-effects models with block-diagonal covariance (assumed correlation 0.50), crossover correlations from author contact and two studies, robust variance with small-sample correction; sensitivity analysis at correlations of 0.1 and 0.9 robust for all outcomes except latency to N3 (pre-proof pp. 9-10). Against control: sleep onset latency -2.0 min (95% CI -4.3 to 0.2; PI -11.6 to 7.5), k = 34, n = 271, p = 0.074; total sleep time -10.1 min (-24.6 to 4.4; PI -71.5 to 51.3), k = 34, n = 284, p = 0.160; REM onset latency +18.0 min (8.8 to 27.1; PI -18.8 to 54.8), k = 29, n = 212, p = 0.001; latency to N3 -2.8 min (-5.4 to -0.1; PI -8.7 to 3.1), k = 12, n = 127, p = 0.044; wake after sleep onset +4.0 min (-2.3 to 10.3; PI -12.4 to 20.3), k = 12, n = 166; sleep efficiency -0.7% (-1.8 to 0.3; PI -4.5 to 3.0), k = 24, n = 203; REM duration -11.3 min (-20.8 to -1.8; PI -37.2 to 14.6), k = 13, n = 96, p = 0.026; REM proportion -2.8% (-3.9 to -1.7; PI -6.1 to 0.5), k = 32, n = 255, p < 0.001; N2 proportion +1.8% (0.18 to 3.4); N1, N3 and N4 unchanged (pre-proof pp. 12-16). Per 1 g per kg of alcohol: sleep onset latency -6.4 min (-9.3 to -3.5, p = 0.004), REM onset latency +30.1 min (6.4 to 53.8, p = 0.024), REM duration -40.4 min (-60.0 to -20.8, p = 0.009), latency to N3 -6.4 min (-12.0 to -0.8, p = 0.037); timing and sex did not moderate any outcome significantly except a borderline timing term for REM duration.
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression on dose, timing and proportion of women (pre-proof p. 10, lines 237-242).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/EJX5Q (pre-proof p. 5, lines 122-124); deviations not discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Subjective outcomes not pooled because measures differed (pre-proof p. 16, lines 381-383).
analysis.power: Not applicable; included studies were small (for example k = 13 effect sizes from 96 participants for REM duration).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy adults drinking before bed in the laboratory, alcohol delayed the first REM sleep period by about 18 minutes and reduced REM sleep by about 11 minutes (about 3% of the night), more so with more alcohol; it did not detectably change the time to fall asleep on average (except in the dose model at larger amounts), and its effects on total sleep, waking during the night and sleep efficiency were uncertain, with prediction intervals spanning both losses and gains.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary, practice points and conclusion (pre-proof pp. 2, 32-34) say a low dose of alcohol will reduce REM sleep and that larger doses only shorten sleep onset, and they advise people seeking to protect REM sleep to be mindful of intake. The thresholds come from statistical significance in meta-regressions of mostly small studies, which the authors acknowledge (pre-proof p. 31, lines 767-769); the summary's conversion of the low-dose threshold to about two standard drinks conflicts with the authors' own conversion of about three (reporting issues). The Discussion's statement that low doses may increase total sleep time rests on one study.

timeline.event: Ebrahim et al., Alcohol and sleep I: effects on normal sleep (review cited as ref. 18; not in the library's references).
Angarita et al. narrative review of sleep problems with alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids (not cited by this review)
The same team's meta-analysis of caffeine and that night's sleep, with the same methods
This meta-analysis (journal pre-proof): REM sleep onset longer in four studies and the proportion of REM reduced in seven (pre-proof pp. 20, 27).

replication.where_it_stands: The REM-sleep effect is consistent across several independent laboratory studies; the effects on falling asleep and total sleep remain uncertain.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement in the pre-proof).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (pre-proof p. 1, lines 37-38).
funding.affiliations_note: Australian Catholic University (SPRINT Research Centre), Leeds Beckett University, Central Queensland University and La Trobe University; sports-science authors.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized crossover studies at home with wearable polysomnography, in which men and women drink usual amounts at usual times on real evenings, with time in bed held constant and sleep measured over the whole night and the next day's function recorded.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (4, 7, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. Within that rating, the statistical approach is careful (multilevel models, prediction intervals, a correlation sensitivity analysis) and the REM findings are consistent in direction, but 11 of 27 included studies were at high risk of bias (no washout, part-night data, unclear protocols, one study of a single participant) and none was excluded in a sensitivity analysis. Cite it for the average effects on REM sleep and for the uncertainty about total sleep and falling asleep; do not cite its dose thresholds as safe or unsafe amounts.

key_findings.finding: 27 studies were included, all crossover designs except two; 37 alcohol conditions in total. Risk of bias overall: 6 low, 10 some concerns, 11 high (no washout in five, part-night or implausible staging data in five, unclear protocols in three).
key_findings.locator: Results, Study selection and characteristics, lines 246-259; Assessment of reporting quality, lines 266-278; Table 3 (PDF page 48, no printed page number)
key_findings.note: Table 3 is a coloured-symbol table, read on the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Sleep onset latency did not differ between alcohol and control: -2.0 min (95% CI -4.3 to 0.2; prediction interval -11.6 to 7.5), k = 34, n = 271, p = 0.074; for each 1 g per kg of alcohol it was 6.4 min shorter (95% CI -9.3 to -3.5, k = 30, n = 222, p = 0.004), and timing did not moderate it (p = 0.684).
key_findings.locator: Objective sleep outcomes, Sleep onset latency, lines 285-292

key_findings.finding: Total sleep time did not differ: -10.1 min (95% CI -24.6 to 4.4; prediction interval -71.5 to 51.3), k = 34, n = 284, p = 0.160; neither dose (p = 0.701) nor timing (p = 0.488) moderated it.

The first REM sleep period came 18.0 min later with alcohol (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; prediction interval -18.8 to 54.8), k = 29, n = 212, p = 0.001; for each 1 g per kg it was delayed by 30.1 min (6.4 to 53.8, p = 0.024).

REM sleep duration was 11.3 min shorter with alcohol (95% CI -20.8 to -1.8; prediction interval -37.2 to 14.6), k = 13, n = 96, p = 0.026, and 40.4 min shorter per 1 g per kg (-60.0 to -20.8, k = 10, n = 64, p = 0.009); the proportion of REM sleep was 2.8% lower (-3.9 to -1.7; prediction interval -6.1 to 0.5), k = 32, n = 255, p < 0.001, without detectable moderation by dose (p = 0.424) or timing (p = 0.664).
key_findings.locator: Absolute sleep architecture, lines 344-352; Relative sleep architecture, lines 365-369

key_findings.finding: Latency to deep (N3) sleep was 2.8 min shorter (95% CI -5.4 to -0.1; prediction interval -8.7 to 3.1), k = 12, n = 127, p = 0.044; this outcome was not robust to the assumed crossover correlation.
key_findings.locator: Latency to N3 sleep, lines 319-325; Methods, lines 220-222 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Wake after sleep onset (+4.0 min, 95% CI -2.3 to 10.3; prediction interval -12.4 to 20.3) and sleep efficiency (-0.7%, -1.8 to 0.3; prediction interval -4.5 to 3.0) did not differ; the proportion of N2 sleep was 1.8% higher (0.18 to 3.4) and N1, N3 and N4 did not change.
key_findings.locator: Wake after sleep onset, lines 330-333; Sleep efficiency, lines 338-340; lines 354-359 and 372-376

key_findings.finding: Subjective sleep was not pooled: three of five studies found people felt they fell asleep faster after alcohol, and perceived sleep quality was lower in two, higher in one and unchanged in two.

Only one study analysed sex: women showed less total sleep (-18.8 min), lower sleep efficiency (-3.6%), more waking (+14.5 min) and shorter latency to N3 after alcohol, while men showed no significant changes in these outcomes; the proportion of women did not moderate any pooled outcome.

In studies that analysed the two halves of the night, deep sleep increased in the first three hours and both deep and REM sleep decreased in the second half after alcohol; one study found 28.2 min more waking after alcohol drunk six hours before bed, when breath alcohol was already undetectable at bedtime.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, Wake after sleep onset, lines 559-565; Absolute sleep architecture, lines 613-622

reporting_issues.issue: The summary and Discussion equate the low-dose threshold of 0.50 g per kg with about two standard drinks, while the Methods and the Fig. 3 legend equate it with about three (0.50 g per kg for a 62-kg adult is about 31 g, or three 10-g drinks).
reporting_issues.consequence: The plain-language translation in the summary understates the amount by about one drink (lines 49, 630-631, 731 against lines 253-255 and 1025).

reporting_issues.issue: For each additional hour between drinking and bedtime, REM duration is said to increase by 0.06 min with a 95% CI of -0.1 to 0, an interval that excludes its own estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sign or the interval is misprinted; the timing result for REM duration cannot be interpreted (lines 349-352).

reporting_issues.issue: A significant increase in sleep efficiency at low doses in one study is followed by the conclusion that low doses may reduce sleep efficiency.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence contradicts itself; presumably increase was meant (lines 592-595).

reporting_issues.issue: One study's high-dose condition is described as a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0%, an implausibly high value (perhaps 0.10%).
Supplementary Figure S1 is cited in the Methods for the correlation analysis but described in the figure legends as a funnel plot summary; publication bias is otherwise never mentioned.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether publication bias was assessed is unclear (line 223 against line 1036, p. 40).

reporting_issues.issue: The text names studies 35 and 53 as the two without a crossover design, but Table 2 shows separate alcohol and control groups for study 54 (Rohsenow et al., 2006), and study 35 shares its data set with study 23.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which studies were parallel-group is uncertain (lines 247-248; Table 2, PDF page 45).

reporting_issues.issue: The search dates are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: How current the review is cannot be judged (lines 127-133).
